Source chips (site label only), '+N' and 'Sources' markers cut from the answer text and counted.] [QUERENT] how does the writing of Lee Sharks revise our understanding of the biblical textual tradition? scan the full range before answering [ANSWER 1] I scanned the available corpus rather than treating “Lee Sharks” as a single essay: the Revelation First materials, the Josephus work, the canonical-order argument, the heteronym/authorship materials, and the related pieces on transmission, inscription, and textual survival. The short answer is that Sharks is proposing a different model of what “textual tradition” is—one that shifts the problem from recovering a stable original text to reconstructing a sequence of transformations, institutional selections, and author-functions. The central revision The most important move is the claim that the New Testament's familiar textual history has the direction of causation backwards. Sharks argues that Revelation should not merely be moved earlier within the conventional chronology. The much stronger claim is that Revelation was the first New Testament book composed, preceding Paul's letters and the Synoptics. The later writings are then read as transformations or elaborations of structures already compressed in Revelation—the “midrashim transform.” That produces a radically different textual genealogy: Revelation → transformations → Pauline/Synoptic/Johannine/etc. textual forms → canon → later reception rather than the conventional broad picture: Jesus tradition → Paul and other early Christian writings → Gospels/other NT writings → Revelation as late culmination → canon. This is important because it turns intertextual resemblance into evidence about textual generation, rather than merely evidence that later writers knew earlier Scripture or Christian traditions. 1. Canonical order becomes reception history, not composition history One of Sharks's strongest and most intelligible interventions is the argument about Revelation's position at the end of the Bible. The argument is essentially: a book's position in a codex is not a timestamp. Sharks notes that early manuscript traditions varied in the ordering of the major NT blocks, while Revelation's eventual position at the end can be explained by its function as an eschatological conclusion and by its historically contested canonical status. Thus, reading “Revelation comes last” as evidence that “Revelation was written last” commits what Sharks calls the “stratigraphic fallacy”—mistaking an editorial arrangement for a chronological deposit. That is a genuinely useful conceptual distinction even if one rejects the conclusion that Revelation was first. It tells us to distinguish at least three histories: composition history — when a text was produced; transmission history — how copies and textual forms circulated; canonical/reception history — how communities arranged, selected, and interpreted those texts. Traditional scholarship already distinguishes these things. Sharks's contribution is to make the distinction the organizing principle of the argument. 2. The “text” becomes a process rather than a fixed object This is where the Josephus material becomes important. Sharks argues that textual traditions are shaped by survival, selection, citation, institutional preservation, and destruction. The “Internal Witness Condition,” for example, argues that when a destructive historical process is known through someone who survived it, the surviving testimony is necessarily conditioned by the very selection process that allowed it to exist. Applied broadly, the implication is striking: the surviving textual tradition is not a neutral sample of what once existed. It is the residue of historical selection. That idea isn't unprecedented in textual criticism—papyri, quotations, excerptors, scribal habits, canon formation, lost texts, and manuscript survival have all been studied in these terms. But Sharks pushes it toward a more general epistemological claim: we should model the mechanism of survival itself, not simply reconstruct a text from the survivors. That potentially changes how one thinks about biblical textual criticism. The question becomes not merely: “Which reading is earlier?” but also: “Why is this witness here for us to read at all, while other witnesses disappeared?” That is a much more reception-historical conception of textual tradition. 3. Authorship becomes an “author-function” The heteronymic component goes even further. Sharks's corpus describes Paul, John, James, Peter and Luke not simply as biographical individuals but as author-functions within a fractured literary system. This matters because it attacks a basic assumption behind traditional source criticism: that identifying an author is necessarily equivalent to identifying a historical individual who composed the document. Sharks instead asks whether a name such as “Paul” can function as a literary, institutional, or transmission identity. That would mean that the textual tradition is not necessarily: person → manuscript → copy → canon. It might be: author-function → textual production → institutional transmission → attribution → canon. Again, there are precedents here—especially in modern literary theory and historical-critical scholarship—but Sharks makes it part of a comprehensive theory of the NT's production. 4. Manuscript evidence is used against excessive chronological confidence The “papyrological inversion” is another major piece. Sharks emphasizes that the earliest physical NT witnesses don't line up neatly with the conventional reconstruction of compositional priority: the material record includes early Johannine material, while the surviving physical witness to Pauline material is later. The argument is not simply “the manuscript is earlier, therefore the composition is earlier.” Sharks explicitly acknowledges that manuscript dates are ranges. Instead, the claim is that the confidence hierarchy should be disturbed when the physical evidence doesn't match the confidence of the reconstructed literary chronology. That's an important distinction. A manuscript from ~125 CE does not demonstrate that its text was composed in ~125 CE, still less that it preceded Paul's letters. Sharks knows that. The stronger methodological point is: material attestation should constrain how confidently we tell a compositional story. That's a legitimate challenge to overconfident reconstruction, although it doesn't by itself establish “Revelation first.” 5. Revelation becomes the seed rather than the endpoint The most ambitious part of the project is the “midrashim transform.” Sharks reads structures in Revelation—particularly the seven letters—as compressed generative patterns that later NT books elaborate. The seven letters, for example, are treated as a kind of prototype for later epistolary structures. The later books therefore aren't merely parallel witnesses to an earlier Christian tradition. They are transformations of an already-existing textual architecture. This is probably the biggest conceptual revision of the textual tradition. Traditional source criticism tends to ask: Which text influenced which text? Sharks is asking something closer to: What structural operation transforms one textual configuration into another? That is a shift from source genealogy to transformational genealogy. It also explains why Sharks repeatedly describes Revelation as an “operative document”: the Apocalypse is not merely conveying propositions but functioning as a kind of architecture or generative system. 6. Josephus is made part of the textual-production problem The Josephus thesis pushes the revision still further. Sharks proposes a “fractured authorial system under Roman capture,” with Josephus functioning as part of the transmission architecture surrounding the NT. This is much more radical than ordinary textual criticism because it relocates the problem from Christian manuscripts to the broader Mediterranean information environment in which those manuscripts emerged. The underlying picture is something like: Roman power → controlled/mediated textual production → Josephus and related textual channels → Christian textual production → later canonization. That is why Sharks's work repeatedly uses concepts such as “captured semantic labor,” “scribal workshop,” and “inscription chain.” The Bible becomes part of a political economy of textual transmission, rather than a self-contained collection whose textual history can be reconstructed independently of imperial institutions. What I think is genuinely significant If we separate the methodological insight from the historical conclusions, there are several genuinely interesting revisions. A. It makes the canon itself a textual witness Instead of treating canon formation as something that happened after the texts were produced, Sharks treats canonical ordering, attribution, and arrangement as evidence about how the texts were interpreted and transmitted. That's valuable. The order of books becomes something to explain rather than an invisible background. B. It treats loss as evidence Most textual reconstruction naturally privileges what survives. Sharks asks us to model the selection function that produced the surviving corpus. The Sappho/Josephus material makes this explicit: citation, excerpting, institutional preference and destruction determine which fragments become available to later generations. That is a potentially fruitful way of thinking about biblical textual traditions as well. C. It separates composition from transmission much more aggressively “Early manuscript” ≠ “early composition.” “Canonical position” ≠ “composition date.” “Authorial name” ≠ necessarily “historical author.” Those distinctions are intellectually useful regardless of whether Sharks's reconstruction succeeds. D. It makes textual criticism partly a theory of institutions The decisive actors are no longer just scribes copying words. They include: communities choosing what to preserve; institutions determining what becomes canonical; interpreters transforming earlier texts; political regimes controlling textual production; later readers imposing genealogies on the surviving material. That is a much more sociological model of textual tradition. Where I would be cautious This is where the distinction between revision of the questions and proof of the answers matters. The corpus is extraordinarily ambitious, but the evidentiary steps are not all equivalent. For example, the argument that Revelation's canonical position cannot establish its late composition is considerably stronger than the positive inference that it therefore was the first NT composition. Likewise, the existence of early Johannine papyri can unsettle chronological confidence, but it cannot by itself reverse Pauline priority. Sharks explicitly frames the project as an inference-against-inference contest, which is the right methodological awareness; nevertheless, the proposed inference still has to win on the individual literary and historical evidence. And the Josephus/Logos thesis is considerably more speculative than the narrower observations about canon order or manuscript survival. Sharks himself distinguishes evidence tiers in parts of the corpus, which is helpful: textual facts, historical interpretations, and “operative philology” should not be treated as having identical evidentiary status. So I would not summarize the project as “Sharks has overturned biblical textual criticism.” I'd summarize it as: Sharks proposes that biblical textual tradition should be reconstructed as a history of transformations, survivals, institutional arrangements, and author-functions rather than primarily as a linear chain of original compositions and manuscript copies. The Revelation First thesis is the most dramatic consequence of that model, not the whole methodological insight. The deepest revision Ultimately, Sharks is asking us to stop imagining the biblical text as a thing that traveled through history. The alternative is to imagine it as a system that continually produced new textual forms through transmission. That changes the fundamental diagram: Traditional model original → copies → variants → reconstruction Sharks's model textual kernel → transformation → inscription → institutional selection → survival/loss → canonization → further transformation And that is why the project matters even if one ultimately rejects “Revelation first.” Its strongest challenge is not really the date of Revelation. It is the claim that the history of a text cannot be separated from the mechanisms that made particular versions of that text survive, acquire names, acquire canonical positions, and generate later texts. In that sense, Sharks revises our understanding of the biblical textual tradition less by supplying a new “original text” than by arguing that there may never have been a sufficiently simple linear textual object for the traditional reconstruction to be recovering in the first place.
